title: THE SIN SO DISTURBING GOD NAMED IT IN THE BIBLE—AND THE WARNING MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER UNDERSTOOD
paragraphs: THE SIN SO DISTURBING GOD NAMED IT IN THE BIBLE—AND THE WARNING MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER UNDERSTOOD

Leviticus 18:23 reveals something far deeper than a forbidden act: why God established boundaries for Israel, what happens when humanity rejects His created order, and how Jesus Christ offers redemption without ever calling evil good.
There are verses in the Bible that comfort us.
Verses we underline when life becomes unbearable. Verses we whisper through tears. Verses we send to someone who is losing hope.
And then there are verses that make us uncomfortable.
Verses we would rather skip.
Verses that confront the things human beings are capable of doing when desire is separated from holiness.
Leviticus 18:23 is one of them.
God gave Israel a command so disturbing that many Christians today have never heard it explained from the pulpit.
He explicitly prohibited sexual relations between human beings and animals.
And before you close this article because the subject feels too shocking, consider something.
Why would a holy God need to say something that should have been unthinkable in the first place?
Why did He include this prohibition among the laws that would distinguish Israel from the nations surrounding them?
And what does a command written thousands of years ago reveal about the human heart sitting behind a smartphone screen today?
Because the deeper question is not simply why God forbade one horrifying act.
The deeper question is what happens when human beings decide that their desires should determine their boundaries.
And if we follow this passage carefully, something extraordinary happens.
A disturbing prohibition begins to reveal the holiness of God.
The holiness of God exposes the rebellion of humanity.
And that rebellion brings us face-to-face with the desperate need for Jesus Christ.
But we must begin where Scripture begins.
Not with outrage.
Not with speculation.
Not with an attempt to make an ancient passage say something it never said.
With the Word of God itself.
Leviticus 18:23 declares in the King James Version:
“Neither shalt thou lie with any beast to defile thyself therewith: neither shall any woman stand before a beast to lie down thereto: it is confusion.”
That final word deserves our attention.
Confusion.
The original Hebrew uses the word תֶּבֶל (tevel).
It is a rare word that, in this context, describes a grave violation of proper boundaries—something perverse or a wrongful mixing of categories that should remain distinct.
The Hebrew does not merely describe an unusual preference or an alternative expression of desire.
It identifies conduct that violates God's established moral order.
Modern translations commonly render the concluding expression as “perversion.”
That distinction matters.
The biblical text is not primarily discussing psychological confusion or claiming that every kind of uncertainty is sinful.
It is condemning a particular sexual act as morally disordered.
And the context makes that unmistakable.
God was establishing boundaries for a people He had redeemed from slavery and called to live differently.
Israel had been brought out of Egypt.
They were not supposed to carry every practice of Egypt into their new life.
Nor were they supposed to imitate every practice of the land of Canaan.
Listen to what God said earlier in the chapter:

“After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do: and after the doings of the land of Canaan, whither I bring you, shall ye not do: neither shall ye walk in their ordinances.” — Leviticus 18:3, KJV
Notice the pattern.
God did not simply tell Israel what to avoid.
He told them whose ways they must not imitate.
Their identity was no longer supposed to be determined by the cultures surrounding them.
Their identity was rooted in the God who had delivered them.
And then, in Leviticus 18:4–5, He called them to walk in His judgments and statutes.
The message was unmistakable.
Redemption was supposed to change how they lived.
That is where this ancient passage begins to become painfully personal.
Because it is possible to leave Egypt geographically while still carrying Egypt in your heart.
It is possible to escape a place of bondage while continuing to love the habits that once enslaved you.
It is possible to say that God has rescued you while resisting the boundaries He establishes for your good.
Israel's challenge was not merely to cross a wilderness.
It was to learn what holiness looked like after deliverance.
And that challenge did not disappear when the wilderness journey ended.
But we need to understand something else.
Leviticus 18 is not a random collection of strange restrictions.
The chapter addresses forbidden sexual relationships, including incestuous relationships, adultery, and other prohibited acts.
The prohibition involving animals appears within that broader moral context.
God was drawing distinctions between legitimate and illegitimate sexual conduct.
He was teaching Israel that human sexuality was not morally unrestricted.
And the prohibition in verse 23 protects a boundary between human beings and animals that Scripture does not permit sexual desire to cross.
Animals are living creatures entrusted to human stewardship, not partners capable of entering the human covenant of marriage.
Genesis 1:26–28 presents humanity as uniquely made in God's image and entrusted with responsibility over other living creatures.
Genesis 2:18–24 presents human companionship and the marriage union within the relationship between man and woman.
These passages provide important creation context for understanding why Scripture distinguishes human sexual relationships from humanity's relationship with animals.
The Bible's prohibition is therefore not merely about social embarrassment or cultural preference.
It belongs to a moral vision in which created distinctions matter and human beings are accountable to their Creator.
And here we must resist the temptation to exaggerate the historical evidence.
Leviticus 18:24–30 connects the chapter's prohibited practices with the defilement of the nations that inhabited the land before Israel.
That is what Scripture says.
But the text does not provide a detailed historical account proving how frequently every individual prohibition was practiced in every neighboring society.
We should not invent sensational stories about ancient rituals or claim that every surrounding nation routinely practiced this particular offense.
The biblical warning is serious enough without embellishment.
God declared these practices defiling.
He warned Israel not to participate in them.
And He connected persistent moral corruption with judgment.
Leviticus 18:25 uses striking language about the land being defiled and expelling its inhabitants.
The imagery is severe.
Sin was not being presented as a harmless private matter.
The covenant people were being warned that rebellion had consequences beyond an individual's immediate desires.
Yet something even more revealing appears in the chapter.
God did not give Israel permission to assume that they were morally superior simply because they belonged to Israel.
They, too, were warned.
They, too, could defile the land.
They, too, could face judgment.
The warning was not, “Those people are terrible, but you are automatically righteous.”
It was, in effect, “You belong to Me. Do not walk in the same rebellion.”
And perhaps that is the part modern believers most urgently need to hear.
Because religious identity is not a substitute for obedience.
A Bible in your home does not automatically mean Scripture governs your decisions.
A Christian name in your social media biography does not automatically mean Christ rules your heart.
A worship song playing in the background does not make hidden rebellion holy.
And knowing the language of grace does not give us permission to make peace with sin.
But before we turn this passage into an accusation against everyone else, we need to be careful.
Leviticus 18:23 condemns a specific act.
It does not authorize us to accuse people without evidence.
It does not justify cruelty, harassment, or the public humiliation of someone who has sinned.
And it certainly does not mean that people who struggle with disturbing thoughts, unwanted impulses, or a painful past are beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Scripture calls evil what it is.
But Scripture also reveals a Savior who came to rescue sinners.
Both truths matter.
Imagine, for a moment, someone sitting alone late at night.
Their phone is in their hand.
Their family believes everything is fine.
Their friends know the version of them that smiles in photographs.
Their church knows the version that says, “I'm blessed.”
But hidden beneath that familiar face is a struggle they are terrified to admit.
Perhaps it is pornography.
Perhaps an affair.
Perhaps a habit that has become a prison.
Perhaps memories of something they did and desperately wish they could undo.
Perhaps something done to them that they never chose and have carried in silence for years.
Those situations are not morally identical.
Someone harmed by another person's abuse is not guilty merely because they were victimized.
And an unwanted thought is not the same thing as a deliberate action.
But the human suffering behind secrecy, shame, temptation, and fear is real.
Some people hide because they are protecting sin.
Others hide because they are afraid no one will understand their pain.
And sometimes the same person is carrying both guilt that needs repentance and wounds that need healing.
This is why we cannot preach holiness without compassion.
And we cannot preach compassion by pretending holiness no longer matters.
The Gospel calls us to something deeper than either condemnation without hope or acceptance without transformation.
It calls us to the truth.
And the truth begins with a God who has the authority to establish boundaries.
Consider how often our culture treats boundaries as enemies of freedom.
If a desire feels powerful, we are tempted to believe it must be legitimate.
If a behavior is consensual between humans, some assume that settles every moral question.
If something is private, we may conclude that no one—including God—has the right to speak about it.
But Scripture does not define righteousness by the intensity of desire.
Nor does it teach that every impulse should be obeyed.
The strength of a desire does not determine its moral legitimacy.
And God's authority does not disappear when His commands become unpopular.
A boundary can be an expression of love.
A parent who keeps a child away from a dangerous road is not declaring war on the child's freedom.
The parent is protecting the child's life.
Of course, that illustration does not mean every human restriction is righteous or that every person claiming divine authority is trustworthy.
Human beings can misuse rules to control and abuse others.
That is why our standard must be God's revealed character and Word, not the arbitrary demands of religious personalities.
The God who establishes moral boundaries is also the God who commands justice, condemns oppression, and cares for the vulnerable.
His holiness is not permission for human cruelty.
And His mercy is not permission for human rebellion.
Now return to the language of Leviticus.
Throughout this chapter, the repeated concern is defilement.
The Hebrew verb טָמֵא (tameʾ) means to become unclean or defiled, depending on context.
In Leviticus 18, the concern is moral defilement associated with prohibited sexual conduct.
This is important because the Bible uses purity language in different ways.
Not every form of ritual uncleanness in the Old Testament was itself a personal sin.
Childbirth, bodily discharges, and contact with the dead could involve ritual impurity under Israel's ceremonial system.
But the forbidden acts in Leviticus 18 are presented as moral violations, not merely temporary ceremonial conditions.
Understanding that distinction protects us from careless interpretation.
It also helps us see why the New Testament's teaching about holiness remains significant.
Christians do not live under the Mosaic covenant as ancient Israel did.
The New Testament teaches that believers are not justified by keeping the Law of Moses.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Yet grace does not erase the moral seriousness of sexual sin.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3, Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “fornication” is πορνεία (porneia), a broad term for sexual immorality.
Paul was not teaching that salvation could be earned through flawless behavior.
He was teaching that those who belong to Christ are called to holiness.
The New Testament does not repeat every individual prohibition from Leviticus 18 in identical language.
But it consistently rejects sexual immorality and calls believers to honor God with their bodies.
And that brings us to a question that is more uncomfortable than the original headline.
What good is it to be shocked by a sin you have never committed while refusing to repent of the sins you practice every day?
It is easy to read Leviticus 18:23 and say, “I would never do that.”
But have you ever used another human being for your own gratification?
Have you ever betrayed someone's trust?
Have you ever fed a secret appetite while telling yourself it was harmless?
Have you ever treated another person as an object rather than someone made in the image of God?
Have you ever defended something simply because surrendering it would cost you?
These questions do not make every sin equally severe.
Scripture recognizes distinctions in conduct, responsibility, and judgment.
But they do expose something we would rather ignore.
We can condemn the sins that disgust us while excusing the sins that comfort us.
We can be deeply offended by someone else's darkness while carefully protecting our own.
And Jesus confronted that kind of hypocrisy.
In Matthew 7:3–5, He warned against noticing the speck in another person's eye while ignoring the beam in our own.
He was not forbidding all moral discernment.
He was confronting self-righteous judgment.
The kind that sees another person's failure clearly but refuses to examine its own heart.
And now the story takes a turn.
Because if Leviticus only showed us what God forbids, we might leave this passage with fear and nothing more.
We might see the seriousness of sin but never understand the possibility of redemption.
We might recognize our guilt without discovering where forgiveness can be found.
But the Bible does not end in Leviticus.
And the story of humanity does not end with our rebellion.
It moves toward a cross.
Toward a Savior.
Toward the One who never compromised holiness and never stopped calling sinners to repentance.
Jesus Christ did not come to announce that sin was imaginary.
He came because sin was real.
He did not suffer because humanity merely needed better self-esteem.
He suffered because humanity needed reconciliation with God.
The cross tells us something that our pride desperately resists.
Our sin is serious enough that we cannot save ourselves.
But God's love is so great that He gave His Son.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
Read that again.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had become respectable.
Not after we had successfully hidden every shameful chapter.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated “repentance.”
It refers to a change of mind or heart that, in the biblical call to repentance, involves turning away from sin and toward God.
Repentance is more than embarrassment over being exposed.
It is more than regret over consequences.
It is a genuine turning toward the Lord.
And faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting Him as Savior and Lord.
That is why the Gospel is not simply a message about escaping punishment.
It is a message about being reconciled to God and transformed by His grace.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:11:
Those words follow a serious warning about unrighteous conduct.
But notice what Paul says to the believers.
“Such were some of you.”
Not because their past never happened.
Not because their sins were insignificant.
But because their identity in Christ was no longer defined solely by what they had once been.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
What extraordinary words for people who knew the weight of their former lives.
And what extraordinary hope for someone reading this who believes their worst chapter has already determined their ending.
Maybe you have never committed the particular offense condemned in Leviticus 18:23.
Maybe you cannot imagine doing so.
But perhaps you know what it means to carry something you are ashamed to confess.
Perhaps you have promised God a hundred times that you would stop a destructive habit.
Perhaps you have wondered whether you have crossed a line beyond which forgiveness is impossible.
Hear what Scripture actually promises.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
That promise is not a license to continue deliberately in sin.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
And if your struggle involves conduct that harms another person or animal, repentance must include stopping that harm and taking responsible steps to protect the vulnerable.
Seeking appropriate professional help, accountability, and pastoral care can be part of that response.
If you have been abused, however, you do not need to repent for the abuse someone inflicted on you.
You deserve safety, support, and care.
The Gospel does not confuse the guilt of the perpetrator with the suffering of the victim.
That distinction is not a concession to modern culture.
It is an expression of biblical justice.
God sees what people do.
And He sees what has been done to people.
He is not indifferent to either.
This is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because consequences magically disappear when someone says a prayer.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem lives that human beings would have written off as hopeless.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the past never happened.
Grace rewrites the future by bringing forgiven sinners into a new relationship with God.
And sometimes the evidence of that transformation is not dramatic.
Sometimes it is a person finally confessing the truth.
Sometimes it is deleting what has been feeding a destructive habit.
Sometimes it is asking for help instead of hiding.
Sometimes it is accepting responsibility without making excuses.
Sometimes it is learning to live faithfully one ordinary day at a time.
Sometimes it is someone who has suffered abuse finally understanding that the shame belongs to the wrongdoer, not the victim.
And sometimes it is a believer discovering that holiness is not the enemy of joy.
It is part of what it means to belong to the God who made us.
There is another Hebrew expression that brings the heart of Leviticus into focus.
In Leviticus 19:2, God commands Israel to be holy because He is holy.
The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh) means “holy,” carrying the idea of being set apart and belonging to what is sacred.
Holiness involves separation from what defiles, but biblical holiness is more than avoidance.
It is belonging to God.
And that changes how we understand His boundaries.
God was not merely building fences around Israel's behavior.
He was forming a people whose lives would reflect their relationship with Him.
A people called to distinguish righteousness from wickedness.
A people commanded to treat life, bodies, relationships, and worship with reverence.
A people who would learn that being redeemed meant they could no longer simply imitate the world around them.
And Christians today should recognize the spiritual principle.
We do not become holy by pretending we have no weaknesses.
We pursue holiness because we belong to Christ.
We confess when we fail.
We receive His forgiveness.
We depend on the Holy Spirit.
And we learn to obey.
Not to purchase salvation.
But because salvation is a gift that changes the direction of our lives.
So what does Leviticus 18:23 ultimately reveal?
It reveals that God's moral boundaries extend even to actions human beings may consider too shocking to discuss.
It reveals that Israel was called to reject practices God identified as defiling.
It reveals that sexuality was never presented in Scripture as an unlimited field for human experimentation.
It reveals that being God's people required more than possessing a religious identity.
And when read within the whole biblical story, it reminds us why humanity needs a Redeemer.
Because the problem of sin cannot be solved by public outrage alone.
Outrage may identify wrongdoing.
But outrage cannot cleanse the conscience.
Public shame cannot regenerate the heart.
And pretending that every desire is good cannot reconcile humanity to a holy God.
Only Jesus Christ can save.
Only His sacrifice is sufficient for our reconciliation with the Father.
Only His grace can forgive and transform sinners who come to Him in faith.
And now I want to ask you something personally.
Not as someone reading an article.
Not as someone scrolling through another controversial subject.
But as a human being standing before God.
Is there a boundary God has established that you have been trying to negotiate instead of obey?
You do not have to tell the internet your private history.
You do not have to expose trauma or confess intimate details in a public comment section.
But you can be honest with God.
If Christ has brought you out of a season of darkness, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness without revealing details that would compromise your safety or another person's privacy.
Someone else may need to know that repentance is possible.
Someone else may need to know that grace is real.
Someone else may need to know that their story is not finished.
And perhaps this is also the right moment to think about what you are helping spread through your own social media presence.
Every day, millions of people share things that entertain, provoke, distract, or divide.
But imagine what could happen if more believers deliberately shared Scripture, thoughtful biblical teaching, and the hope of the Gospel.
Not to win arguments.
Not to embarrass sinners.
Not to build a reputation for religious superiority.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of being proclaimed.
Someone who has questions about Christianity.
Someone struggling with shame.
Someone who has become spiritually indifferent.
Someone who needs to encounter both the seriousness of sin and the extraordinary mercy of Christ.
The goal is not merely to increase an audience.
The goal is to keep pointing people toward the Word of God and the Savior revealed through it.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and expand, there is a deeper way to participate.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical teaching and discipleship resources accessible to people who are hungry to grow in their relationship with Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of a continuing effort to encourage biblical literacy, spiritual growth, repentance, and faithful Christian living.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry requires time, work, resources, and the generosity of people who believe in its mission.

It is a voluntary act of support that can help sustain the creation and distribution of Christ-centered teaching, expand the ministry's reach, and strengthen the availability of discipleship resources.
For believers who prayerfully choose to include this support in their monthly giving, it can be an expression of generosity and an offering toward Gospel ministry.
But we want to be biblically clear.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You glorify Him through faith, obedience, love, generosity, and a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
But the greatest value of supporting Gospel ministry is not a product or a discount.
It is the opportunity to participate in work that points people toward Jesus.
Because the mission belongs to Christ.
And the glory belongs to God.
Now, before you leave, return with me to the verse that started this entire conversation.
Leviticus 18:23.
A difficult command.
A disturbing subject.
An ancient warning about boundaries that human beings were never authorized to erase.
At first, it may have seemed like a passage with little relevance to your life.
But look where it has taken us.
From God's holiness to human rebellion.
From the danger of unchecked desire to the responsibility of obedience.
From the shame of hidden sin to the hope of repentance.
From the boundaries established in the Law to the mercy revealed in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the greatest surprise is this:
The passage did not simply invite us to examine a sin that most people would find horrifying.
It invited us to examine whether we truly believe that God has the right to tell us how to live.
That question reaches every heart.
Including mine.
Including yours.
The answer is not found in pretending we are better than everyone else.
It is found in surrendering to the One who is holy.
Jesus Christ did not come to make rebellion respectable.
He came to save rebels and make them new.
He did not die so that we could rename darkness as light.
He died and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and brought into the light.
So do not walk away from this passage merely feeling disgust toward someone else's sin.
Walk away with reverence for God.
With compassion for the wounded.
With a renewed commitment to protect the vulnerable.
With courage to confess what needs to be confessed.
With faith in the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
And with the determination to follow Jesus even when His Word challenges what the world has taught you to accept.
Because one day, the opinions of the crowd will no longer matter.
The applause will fade.
The arguments will end.
The screen will go dark.
And what will matter is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
The most frightening thing is not discovering how far sin can take a person—it is discovering how long we can resist the Savior who is calling us home.
